metadata.note: The Nancy Hanks II, the Central of Georgia Railway's Atlanta-Macon-Savannah streamliner and the best known train the road ever ran. She made her first trip on July 17 1947, covering the 293.7 miles in 5 hours 55 minutes southbound and 6 hours northbound as of the 1954 timetable -- close to a 50 mph average on a route that ran down through Barnesville, Forsyth and Macon and then east across the coastal plain by Gordon, Tennille and Millen. The equipment was American Car and Foundry streamlined stock in blue and grey, usually four or five cars: a baggage-coach, a grill lounge and two or three 56-seat coaches. The name goes back to a trotting mare, Nancy Hanks, herself named for Abraham Lincoln's mother, and to an earlier Central of Georgia steam flyer that carried the name briefly in 1892 and 1893 -- hence the II. She made her last run on April 30 1971, the day before Amtrak began, and Amtrak did not take the route: there has been no passenger train between Atlanta and Savannah since.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Hanks_(train) -- Central of Georgia Railway, Atlanta-Savannah via Macon; first trip July 17 1947; 293.7 miles; 5 hours 55 minutes southbound and 6 hours northbound in 1954; last run April 30 1971; named for the racehorse, itself named for Lincoln's mother; an earlier Nancy Hanks ran in 1892-1893.

https://www.american-rails.com/nancyhanks.html -- consist and route detail: ACF streamlined equipment in blue and grey, typically a baggage-coach, grill lounge and two or three 56-seat coaches; roughly a six-hour Atlanta-Savannah run through Barnesville.
https://www.hmdb.org/m.asp?m=186700 -- 'Streamliner Nancy Hanks II' historical marker.

Geometry: OpenStreetMap route relations 2195270 (Norfolk Southern Griffin District, the ex-Central of Georgia Atlanta-Macon line) and 2195277 (Norfolk Southern Savannah District, the ex-Central of Georgia Macon-Savannah main line), fetched via the OSM API 2026-08-24.
not_yet_sourced: The 1892-1893 original Nancy Hanks is not drawn. It ran over much the same route, but its operator was the Central Railroad and Banking Company of Georgia -- the Central of Georgia Railway was not formed until 1895 -- so drawing it would need a separate company and colour, and no month-level dates for its brief run were found.
Only the 1954 timing is sourced. The train's schedule in 1947 and in its final years is not, so the single avg_speed_kmh here stands for the whole 24-year run.
The headway of 720 minutes assumes one train each way per day, which is how the sources describe the service; no timetable page was consulted to confirm it never ran more often.
Intermediate stops beyond the towns used to anchor the trace (Atlanta, East Point, Jonesboro, Griffin, Barnesville, Forsyth, Macon, Gordon, Tennille, Millen, Savannah) are not established.

properties.speed_source: computed from the documented schedule: 293.7 miles in 5 h 55 m southbound / 6 h 00 m northbound (1954 timetable), a 49.3 mph average -- sourced, not estimated
properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap: the ex-Central of Georgia route survives in full as Norfolk Southern's Griffin District (Atlanta-Macon) and Savannah District (Macon-Savannah), and the line is routed leg by leg over those two OSM route relations through Griffin, Barnesville, Macon, Gordon, Tennille and Millen. 3794 points, 288.5 miles against a documented 293.7 -- 1.8% under, the difference being terminal trackage at each end. The trace passes within 117 m of Atlanta, 45 m of East Point, 131 m of Jonesboro, 61 m of Barnesville, 109 m of Gordon, 227 m of Tennille and 334 m of Millen. No straight-line approximation was added. RESOLUTION CAVEAT: 40.9 miles (14%) of the drawn length sits in vertex-to-vertex hops longer than 1 km, with the longest at 2.1 km -- that is how coarsely OSM digitizes rural Georgia trackage, not an approximation introduced here. The corridor and the mileage are right; the fine curvature between those vertices is not resolved. Straight-line repair 2026-08-29: 1 ruled segment totalling 20 mi replaced with OpenStreetMap-traced rail geometry (see geometry_repairs for the OSM lines each one followed).

segments.note: Inaugurated July 17 1947 with American Car and Foundry streamlined equipment in blue and grey -- a baggage-coach, a grill lounge and two or three 56-seat coaches. Scheduled at 5 hours 55 minutes southbound and 6 hours northbound over 293.7 miles as of 1954, roughly a 50 mph average. The name was revived from a Central of Georgia steam flyer of 1892-93, which in turn took it from the trotting mare Nancy Hanks, named for Abraham Lincoln's mother. She ran for the last time on April 30 1971, the day before Amtrak began, and Amtrak did not pick up the route -- Atlanta and Savannah have had no passenger train since. Headway of one train each way per day.
